newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament passes securities trading bill.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament passes securities trading bill.

text.p: The lower house of the Polish parliament on Friday passed a bill on public securities trading adjusting the country's law to international standards and streamlining some formal procedures, the Sejm speaker said.

Deputies voted overwhelmingly in favour of the bill which creates a legal framework for derivatives trading, authorizes brokers to advise their clients and makes issuing new stock easier for listed companies.
Deputies voted 328 against just four abstentions for the new law.

The bill is seen as a part of adjustment of Poland's law to European Union and OECD standards following the country's accession to the Paris-based club of most industrialised nations and ahead of EU accession entry talks.

"It's a big step forward, it paves the way for derivatives, trade, we are closer to European standards and to a free flow of capital," said Sebastian Buczek, the president of Polish brokers union told Reuters.
The bill has yet to be approved by the Senate and signed into law by the president. Expected to provoke little controversy. it could come into force in two months.
It allows Polish companies to float up to 25 percent of shares abroad without the Securities Commission's permission, either directly or through depositary receipts.
After the year 2000, the firms would be allowed to float unlimited stock abroad without a permit.
The bill also provides for companies traded publicly for more than 36 months to issue new shares without submitting issue prospectuses for Securities Commission approval.

According to the new bill only banks, brokerages and insurance firms would be allowed to underwrite issues, unlike the current legislation which allows any firm or even an individual to underwrite an issue.
Analysts said, however it would take several months before the effects of the new law could be seen on the market.

"Surely the effect will be that the capital market will offer more, but one shouldn't expect radical changes immediately...but later maybe derivatives, maybe short selling," said Grzegorz Cimochowski, an analyst at ING Barings.
The new law also lets foreign brokerages open branches in Poland rather than having to register separate firms and allows for the creation of close-ended investment funds.
It also gives Polish citizens the opportunity to buy shares on international markets.

The bill lays ground for the privatisation of the Warsaw bourse, so far acting as a non-profit organisation controlled by the state treasury, by allowing bourse members to earmark up to 20 percent of profit for dividend.

The bill drew criticism from the head of the nascent regulated over-the-counter market Centralna Tabela Ofert (CeTO) who said it upheld too stringent requirements for the OTC market, making raising capital there too costly.
"We are defending small and medium-sized enterprises, which dynamically develop and need capital," Czeslaw Gawlowski told Dziennik Prawa i Gospodarki on Wednesday.
